rationale:
Split into three children. The supplied proof of deformation_good_center follows Simon's proof of 5.1, printed (1)–(7), with the parent's errata. It combines three different techniques, and each is a genuine, separately usable lemma with a clean interface:
(1) tube_cover. The σ-neighbourhood of the dual skeleton L(a) lies in periodic coordinate cylinders. This is the printed identity after (5), parent Step 1; only the inclusion ⊆ is needed.
(2) periodic_maximal. The 5-times covering (Vitali) estimate for the bad set of centres: printed (1)–(4), parent Steps 2–3. It is stated for an arbitrary finite measure on a measurable space X pushed through a measurable map p : X → EuclideanSpace ℝ ι, with the explicit bound 10^k/β.
(3) cylinder_volume. The Fubini–Tonelli bound of the corrected printed (5), parent Step 4.

None of the children depends on another. The parent keeps printed (6)–(7) (parent Steps 5–6) as its own assembly, restated with the children's constants:
- Let 𝒥 := {J ⊆ {1,…,d} : |J| = m+2}, N := |𝒥| ≥ 1, q := (1/2,…,1/2), V := L^d(B_{1/4}(q)) ∈ (0,∞), β := (2N·10^{m+2}+1)/V and c := Nβ. Then 2N·10^{m+2}/β < V.
- For μ ∈ {μ₁, μ₂} and J ∈ 𝒥:
  - p_J(x) := (x_i)_{i∈J} ∈ EuclideanSpace ℝ J;
  - Bad_J(μ) is the bad set of dgc_periodic_maximal with ι = J, X = ℝ^d, p = p_J and g₀ = p_J(q);
  - A_J(μ) := {a ∈ [0,1]^d : p_J(a) ∈ Bad_J(μ)}.
- dgc_cylinder_volume followed by dgc_periodic_maximal gives L^d(A_J(μ)) ≤ 10^{m+2}/β. Hence L^d(⋃_{J∈𝒥}(A_J(μ₁) ∪ A_J(μ₂))) ≤ 2N·10^{m+2}/β < V, so some a ∈ B_{1/4}(q) ⊆ [0,1]^d lies in no A_J(μ_i).
- Then Σ_i(a_i − 1/2)² = |a − q|² < 1/16 and |p_J(a) − p_J(q)| ≤ |a − q| < 1/4. So p_J(a) ∉ Bad_J(μ_i) means μ_i(T_J(p_J(a),σ)) ≤ βσ^{m+2}μ_i(ℝ^d) for every σ ∈ (0,1/4).
- dgc_tube_cover (with d = m+1+ℓ and k = m+2 ≤ d, since ℓ ≥ 1) gives {x : dist(x,La) < σ} ⊆ ⋃_{J∈𝒥} T_J(p_J(a),σ). Subadditivity over the N sets J then gives μ_i({dist(·,La) < σ}) ≤ Nβσ^{m+2}μ_i(ℝ^d) = c·σ^{m+2}·μ_i(ℝ^d).

The children differ from the printed argument only in constants and measurability:
- Lebesgue measure of a closed ball is bounded via ω_k ≤ 2^k.
- The Fubini fibre is bounded by the unit cube instead of an (ℓ−1)-ball.
- Outer Lebesgue measure replaces the Borel property of B_J (parent Step 2), which is then not needed.
- Countability of the disjoint subfamily is shown from disjoint sets of positive measure in a finite measure space.

The split is not atomic and does not solve another DAG node: every child serves this node's own argument, and the parent assembly was kernel-checked.

subproblems.title: σ-tubes about the dual skeleton L(a) lie in periodic coordinate cylinders (printed identity after (5) of 5.1)
subproblems.statement: Let d, k ∈ ℕ with k ≤ d, let a ∈ ℝ^d = Eucl d (Euclidean distance) and L := {y ∈ ℝ^d : there is J ⊆ {1,…,d} with |J| = k and y_i − a_i ∈ ℤ for all i ∈ J}. If σ ∈ ℝ, x ∈ ℝ^d and dist(x, L) < σ, where dist(x, L) = inf_{y∈L}|x − y| (Mathlib infDist), then there are J ⊆ {1,…,d} with |J| = k and integers z_i (i ∈ J) such that Σ_{i∈J}(x_i − a_i − z_i)² < σ², i.e. x ∈ p_J⁻¹(B_σ(p_J(a) + z)) with z = Σ_{i∈J} z_i e_i and p_J the orthogonal projection onto S_J = span{e_i : i ∈ J}.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (d k : ℕ), k ≤ d → ∀ (a : Eucl d) (La : Set (Eucl d)), La = {y | ∃ J : Finset (Fin d), J.card = k ∧ ∀ i ∈ J, ∃ n : ℤ, y i - a i = n} → ∀ (σ : ℝ) (x : Eucl d), infDist x La < σ → ∃ J : Finset (Fin d), J.card = k ∧ ∃ z : J → ℤ, ∑ i : J, (x i - a i - z i) ^ 2 < σ ^ 2
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, §5, printed "Proof of the Deformation Theorem" (p. 164), the identity L_{k−1}(a; σ) = ⋃_{j=1}^{N} ⋃_{z ∈ ℤ^{n+ℓ} ∩ S_j} p_j⁻¹(B_σ(p_j(a) + z)) printed after (5), inclusion "⊆" only, as in Step 1 of the parent proof. In the parent application the present d is n + ℓ and the present k is n + 1 = m + 2, so L is the book's L_{k−1}(a), read as L_{ℓ−1}(a) by the erratum book k = ℓ. Notation: |·| is the Euclidean norm of ℝ^d = Eucl d, and dist(x, L) = inf_{y ∈ L} |x − y| (Mathlib infDist).

1. L is nonempty. Since k ≤ d there is J₀ ⊆ {1,…,d} with |J₀| = k (for instance the first k indices). For every i ∈ J₀, a_i − a_i = 0 ∈ ℤ, so a ∈ L.
2. A point of L near x. Because L ≠ ∅ and inf_{y ∈ L} |x − y| = dist(x, L) < σ, the definition of the infimum gives y ∈ L with |x − y| < σ.
3. Lattice coordinates of y. Since y ∈ L there are J ⊆ {1,…,d} with |J| = k and, for each i ∈ J, an integer n_i with y_i − a_i = n_i. Put z_i := n_i for i ∈ J.
4. For each i ∈ J: x_i − a_i − z_i = x_i − a_i − (y_i − a_i) = x_i − y_i.
5. Using step 4, the nonnegativity of squares, J ⊆ {1,…,d}, the Euclidean formula |x − y|² = Σ_{i=1}^{d} (x_i − y_i)² and 0 ≤ |x − y| < σ:
   Σ_{i∈J} (x_i − a_i − z_i)² = Σ_{i∈J} (x_i − y_i)² ≤ Σ_{i=1}^{d} (x_i − y_i)² = |x − y|² < σ².
6. Hence J (with |J| = k) and the integers (z_i)_{i∈J} have the required property. In the printed notation, z := Σ_{i∈J} z_i e_i ∈ ℤ^d ∩ S_J and p_J(x) ∈ B_σ(p_J(a) + z), i.e. x ∈ p_J⁻¹(B_σ(p_J(a) + z)). ∎
proof_key_steps: L ≠ ∅: since k ≤ d some J₀ has |J₀| = k, and a ∈ L.
dist(x, L) < σ and L ≠ ∅ give y ∈ L with |x − y| < σ.
y ∈ L gives J with |J| = k and integers z_i = y_i − a_i (i ∈ J).
Σ_{i∈J}(x_i − a_i − z_i)² = Σ_{i∈J}(x_i − y_i)² ≤ |x − y|² < σ².

subproblems.title: The bad set of centres has small Lebesgue measure (printed (1)–(4) of 5.1, 5-times covering)
subproblems.statement: Let ι be a finite index set with k := |ι| elements, E := ℝ^ι = EuclideanSpace ℝ ι with its Euclidean distance and Lebesgue measure L^k, (X, 𝒜) a measurable space, μ a finite measure on X, p : X → E measurable, g₀ ∈ E and β > 0. For g ∈ E and σ ∈ ℝ let T(g, σ) := {x ∈ X : there is z ∈ ℤ^ι with Σ_{i∈ι}(p(x)_i − g_i − z_i)² < σ²} (for σ > 0 this equals p⁻¹(⋃_{z∈ℤ^ι} B_σ(g + z))). Let Bad be the set of g ∈ E with |g − g₀| < 1/4 for which some σ with 0 < σ < 1/4 satisfies βσ^k·μ(X) < μ(T(g, σ)) (in [0, ∞]). Then L^k(Bad) ≤ 10^k/β, where L^k(Bad) is the outer Lebesgue measure (Bad is not assumed measurable).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (ι : Type) [Fintype ι] (X : Type) [MeasurableSpace X] (μ : Measure X), IsFiniteMeasure μ → ∀ p : X → EuclideanSpace ℝ ι, Measurable p → ∀ (g₀ : EuclideanSpace ℝ ι) (β : ℝ), 0 < β → volume {g : EuclideanSpace ℝ ι | dist g g₀ < 1 / 4 ∧ ∃ σ : ℝ, 0 < σ ∧ σ < 1 / 4 ∧ ENNReal.ofReal (β * σ ^ Fintype.card ι) * μ univ < μ {x | ∃ z : ι → ℤ, ∑ i, (p x i - g i - z i) ^ 2 < σ ^ 2}} ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (10 ^ Fintype.card ι / β)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, §5, printed "Proof of the Deformation Theorem", displays (1)–(4) and the estimate L^{n+1}(B_j) ≤ β⁻¹5^{n+1}ω_{n+1} that follows them (pp. 163–164), as reproduced in Steps 2–3 of the parent proof, with M(T ⌞ p_j⁻¹(·)) replaced by μ(p⁻¹(·)) for an arbitrary finite measure μ on X and measurable p : X → E (in the parent: X = ℝ^{n+ℓ}, μ = μ₁ or μ₂, E ≅ S_J via p = p_J, k = n + 1 = m + 2, g₀ = x_J = p_J(q)). Bad is the printed bad set B_j = (F_j ∩ B_{1/4}(x_j)) ∖ G_j with B_{1/4}(x_j) taken about g₀. Errata and details: the 5-times covering lemma (Simon Ch. 1, 3.4) is applied to closed balls; disjointness of the periodic tubes is proved as in Step 3 of the parent; the printed ω_k(5σ)^k is bounded by (10σ)^k (ω_k ≤ 2^k; the printed constants are not needed); measurability of Bad (Step 2 of the parent) is not needed, since the estimate is for the outer Lebesgue measure, which is countably subadditive on arbitrary sets.

Notation. For g ∈ E and z ∈ ℤ^ι write g + z for the point (g_i + z_i)_{i∈ι} of E; B_r(c) and B̄_r(c) are the open and closed Euclidean balls of E. Since |w − (g + z)|² = Σ_i (w_i − g_i − z_i)², T(g, σ) = p⁻¹(⋃_{z∈ℤ^ι} B_σ(g + z)) for every σ > 0 (only such σ occur below).

1. The tubes are measurable. For fixed g, σ and z the function w ↦ Σ_i (w_i − g_i − z_i)² is continuous on E, so {w ∈ E : Σ_i (w_i − g_i − z_i)² < σ²} is open. The union U(g, σ) over z ∈ ℤ^ι of these sets is open, hence Borel, and T(g, σ) = p⁻¹(U(g, σ)) is measurable because p is measurable.
2. The case μ(X) = 0. Then μ(T(g, σ)) ≤ μ(X) = 0 = βσ^k μ(X) for all g and σ, so the strict inequality in the definition of Bad never holds. Thus Bad = ∅ and L^k(Bad) = 0 ≤ 10^k/β. From now on assume μ(X) > 0; moreover μ(X) < ∞ because μ is finite.
3. Choice of radii (printed (3)). For each b ∈ Bad fix σ_b with 0 < σ_b < 1/4 and βσ_b^k μ(X) < μ(T(b, σ_b)).
4. Covering (printed (4)). The closed balls B̄_{σ_b}(b), b ∈ Bad, have radii at most 1/4. By the 5-times covering lemma (Simon Ch. 1, 3.4; the Vitali covering lemma, valid in every metric space for a family of closed balls with bounded radii) there is u ⊆ Bad such that the balls B̄_{σ_b}(b), b ∈ u, are pairwise disjoint and every B̄_{σ_g}(g), g ∈ Bad, is contained in B̄_{5σ_b}(b) for some b ∈ u. As g ∈ B̄_{σ_g}(g), we get Bad ⊆ ⋃_{b∈u} B̄_{5σ_b}(b).
5. The tubes of the subfamily are pairwise disjoint (printed: "p_j⁻¹ B_{σ_ℓ}(b_ℓ + z), ℓ = 1, 2, …, z ∈ ℤ^{n+ℓ} ∩ S_j, is a pairwise disjoint collection"). Let b ≠ b′ be in u and suppose x ∈ T(b, σ_b) ∩ T(b′, σ_{b′}). With y := p(x) there are z, z′ ∈ ℤ^ι with |y − (b + z)| < σ_b and |y − (b′ + z′)| < σ_{b′}.
   (a) If z = z′, the point w := y − z (coordinates y_i − z_i) satisfies |w − b| = |y − (b + z)| < σ_b and |w − b′| = |y − (b′ + z)| < σ_{b′}, so w ∈ B̄_{σ_b}(b) ∩ B̄_{σ_{b′}}(b′), contradicting the disjointness in step 4.
   (b) If z ≠ z′: as b, b′ ∈ Bad, |b − g₀| < 1/4 and |b′ − g₀| < 1/4, and σ_b, σ_{b′} < 1/4. Hence |y − (g₀ + z)| ≤ |y − (b + z)| + |b − g₀| < 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 and similarly |y − (g₀ + z′)| < 1/2, i.e. B_{σ_b}(b + z) ⊆ B_{1/2}(g₀ + z) and B_{σ_{b′}}(b′ + z′) ⊆ B_{1/2}(g₀ + z′). Therefore |z − z′| = |(g₀ + z) − (g₀ + z′)| ≤ |(g₀ + z) − y| + |y − (g₀ + z′)| < 1. But z_i ≠ z′_i for some i, and then |z − z′| ≥ |z_i − z′_i| ≥ 1 because z_i − z′_i is a nonzero integer. Contradiction.
6. u is countable. The sets T(b, σ_b), b ∈ u, are measurable (step 1), pairwise disjoint (step 5) and of positive measure, because μ(T(b, σ_b)) > βσ_b^k μ(X) ≥ 0 (step 3). For each integer j ≥ 1, any finitely many of them with measure > 1/j have total measure ≤ μ(X) < ∞, so there are at most j·μ(X) of them; hence only countably many members of the family have positive measure. Since all of them do, u is countable.
7. Summation of (3) (printed: β Σ_ℓ σ_ℓ^{n+1} M(T) ≤ M(T)). By step 3, countable additivity of μ (u is countable, the T(b, σ_b) are measurable and pairwise disjoint) and monotonicity,
   Σ_{b∈u} βσ_b^k μ(X) ≤ Σ_{b∈u} μ(T(b, σ_b)) = μ(⋃_{b∈u} T(b, σ_b)) ≤ μ(X).
   Dividing by μ(X) ∈ (0, ∞) gives Σ_{b∈u} σ_b^k ≤ β⁻¹.
8. Volume of a ball. For c ∈ E and r ≥ 0, every w ∈ B̄_r(c) satisfies |w_i − c_i| ≤ |w − c| ≤ r for each i, so B̄_r(c) ⊆ ∏_{i∈ι} [c_i − r, c_i + r]. Lebesgue measure on E is the product Lebesgue measure in the coordinates, hence L^k(B̄_r(c)) ≤ (2r)^k (printed: ω_k r^k, and ω_k ≤ 2^k).
9. Conclusion (printed L^{n+1}(B_j) ≤ β⁻¹5^{n+1}ω_{n+1}). By step 4, countable subadditivity of the outer Lebesgue measure over the countable set u (step 6), step 8 with r = 5σ_b, and step 7:
   L^k(Bad) ≤ Σ_{b∈u} L^k(B̄_{5σ_b}(b)) ≤ Σ_{b∈u} (10σ_b)^k = 10^k Σ_{b∈u} σ_b^k ≤ 10^k/β. ∎
proof_key_steps: T(g, σ) is measurable (for σ > 0 it equals p⁻¹(⋃_z B_σ(g + z))); if μ(X) = 0 then Bad = ∅.
For b ∈ Bad choose σ_b ∈ (0, 1/4) with βσ_b^k μ(X) < μ(T(b, σ_b)) (printed (3)).
5-times covering: a disjoint subfamily {B̄_{σ_b}(b)}_{b∈u} with Bad ⊆ ⋃_{b∈u} B̄_{5σ_b}(b) (printed (4)).
The tubes T(b, σ_b), b ∈ u, are pairwise disjoint: equal z contradicts the ball disjointness; distinct z is impossible as B_{σ_b}(b + z) ⊆ B_{1/2}(g₀ + z).
u is countable (disjoint sets of positive measure in a finite measure space), and summing (3) gives Σ_{b∈u} σ_b^k ≤ 1/β.

subproblems.title: Fubini bound for the cylinder over a set of centres (corrected printed (5) of 5.1)
subproblems.statement: Let ι be a finite index set and J ⊆ ι, let E_ι := EuclideanSpace ℝ ι and E_J := EuclideanSpace ℝ J carry their Lebesgue measures L^ι and L^J, and let π_J : E_ι → E_J, π_J(a) := (a_i)_{i∈J}. Then for every set B ⊆ E_J (not necessarily measurable), L^ι({a ∈ E_ι : 0 ≤ a_i ≤ 1 for all i ∈ ι, and π_J(a) ∈ B}) ≤ L^J(B), both sides being outer Lebesgue measures.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (ι : Type) [Fintype ι] (J : Finset ι) (B : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ J)), volume {a : EuclideanSpace ℝ ι | (∀ i, 0 ≤ a i ∧ a i ≤ 1) ∧ WithLp.toLp 2 (fun i : J => a i) ∈ B} ≤ volume B
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, §5, printed "Proof of the Deformation Theorem", display (5) (p. 164), in the corrected form of Step 4 of the parent proof (erratum (vi): the printed measure estimate (5) is replaced by a Fubini–Tonelli bound L^{n+ℓ}({a ∈ B_{1/4}(q) : p_j(a) ∈ B_j}) ≤ L^{n+1}(B_j)·(measure of a fibre)). Here the fibres are bounded by the unit cube [0,1]^{ι∖J}, of measure 1, instead of an (ℓ−1)-dimensional ball; in the parent application ι = {1,…,n+ℓ}, J is the index set of S_j (|J| = n + 1), B = B_j, and B_{1/4}(q) ⊆ [0,1]^{n+ℓ}.

Notation: ι∖J := {i ∈ ι : i ∉ J}; Q := {a ∈ E_ι : 0 ≤ a_i ≤ 1 for all i ∈ ι}; S := {a ∈ Q : π_J(a) ∈ B}; ℝ^A carries the product Lebesgue measure λ_A := ⊗_{i∈A} L¹ (for A = ∅ this is the unit point mass).

1. Coordinates. The coordinate map E_ι → ℝ^ι, a ↦ (a_i)_{i∈ι}, is a measurable bijection with measurable inverse which carries L^ι to λ_ι (the Lebesgue measure of EuclideanSpace is the product measure in coordinates); likewise E_J → ℝ^J carries L^J to λ_J. The restriction map ℝ^ι → ℝ^J × ℝ^{ι∖J}, f ↦ (f|_J, f|_{ι∖J}), is a measurable bijection with measurable inverse carrying λ_ι to the product measure λ_J ⊗ λ_{ι∖J} (the product measure over ι splits into the products over J and over ι∖J). Let e : E_ι → ℝ^J × ℝ^{ι∖J} be the composite. Then e is a measure-preserving measurable bijection with measurable inverse, so L^ι(e⁻¹(Z)) = (λ_J ⊗ λ_{ι∖J})(Z) for every set Z (for a measurable equivalence this holds for arbitrary, not necessarily measurable, sets).
2. A rectangle containing S. Let B′ := {g ∈ ℝ^J : the point of E_J with coordinates g lies in B} and C := [0,1]^{ι∖J}. If a ∈ S, then e(a) = ((a_i)_{i∈J}, (a_i)_{i∈ι∖J}); here (a_i)_{i∈J} ∈ B′ because π_J(a) ∈ B, and (a_i)_{i∈ι∖J} ∈ C because a ∈ Q. Hence S ⊆ e⁻¹(B′ × C).
